title: Towards understanding and monitorability of reasoning LLMs - Nature Machine Intelligence
text:
Download PDF

Frontier LLMs are trained to solve problems in a step-by-step way, generating reasoning text in human-understandable language. However, these reasoning tokens are not accurate explanations of LLMs’ internal computations, raising challenges for monitorability.

Large language models (LLMs) have advanced at a remarkable pace in recent years. Arguably, the starting point was 2017, when a new neural network architecture known as the ‘transformer’ was proposed that enabled pre-training on large amounts of natural language data1. Shortly after, around 2018, LLMs BERT (Bidirectional Encoder from Transformer) and GPT (Generative Pretrained Transformer) were built by Google and OpenAI, respectively. In 2019, OpenAI unveiled GPT-2, which excelled at generating human-like text.Around 2024, frontier LLMs became ‘reasoning’ models; to solve complex problems, LLMs are instructed to take several intermediate steps before giving an answer. This method, called chain-of-thought (CoT) generation, was originally proposed as a prompting technique2, but from around 2024, frontier models were trained to include CoT reasoning. Among others, OpenAI released its o1 model, also nicknamed ‘strawberry’, referring to the surprisingly difficult task for LLMs, at least until 2024, of answering the question of “how many ‘r’s’ are in the word: strawberry”.With emerging capabilities to solve multi-step problems with CoT reasoning, users started to deploy LLMs in multi-LLM frameworks to interact, reason and debate with each other. This has enabled, for instance, the development of deep research agents, which can generate scientific hypotheses and propose experimental tests3,4.Although the term ‘reasoning models’ is by now widely adopted, it represents an anthropomorphic framing. This practice is hard to avoid, given that LLMs are trained to use natural language and produce human-like text. Yet the tokens generated by an LLM may not accurately reflect the computations underlying its answer5, raising concerns that CoT reasoning can create an illusion of interpretability. In a recent survey of around 1,000 preprints, AI safety researchers found that, in 25% of papers, authors explicitly treated CoT as an interpretability technique, including in high-stakes domains such as clinical decision making6.In a Perspective in this issue, Levy et al. examine the problem that reasoning tokens are not faithful explanations and explore more intuitive ways of interpreting them. To illustrate how LLMs generate reasoning text, the authors describe the following scenario: imagine someone has to solve a problem on a whiteboard, but every 10 seconds their memory is wiped clean and they can add one word on the whiteboard until the problem is solved. What will be written on the whiteboard is unlikely to be an accurate explanation of the reasoning process, but instead a mixture of shorthand text notes, partial answers and anything else to progress to an answer from cycle to cycle.Keeping this analogy in mind, Levy et al. propose that reasoning tokens are an externalization of the LLM’s computational state, which evolves between generation cycles. But there is no reason to assume that what is externalized, although expressed in human-understandable language as a result of the LLM’s training, is a faithful account of the underlying computation. Indeed, the output text may provide an incomplete account, and moreover, the words used may not carry the same meanings that a human reader attributes to them.Levy et al. propose to adopt a ‘State over Tokens’ (SoT) perspective, interpreting tokens not as a linguistic narrative but as a medium to carry the LLMs’ computational state. As the authors highlight, this view reframes the challenge of interpreting LLMs around new questions: how the computational state is constructed, and how the LLM determines what information to externalize or what tokens to produce. A more complete understanding of these processes would support safety monitoring of frontier models, an issue receiving increasing attention.In a joint position paper last year, researchers from several AI companies (including Google DeepMind, OpenAI and Anthropic) identified CoT reasoning as a potential tool to inspect AI alignment, but at the same time recognized this ‘monitorability’ as a fragile capability given that reasoning traces do not accurately represent the reasoning process7. Dated 3 September 2026, the system card of OpenAI’s new, most capable model, GPT-6 Astra, mentions concerns about monitorability, as the model was found to be able to control its chain-of-thought output much more than previous GPT models. For short tasks, GPT-6 Astra could generate completely unrelated reasoning text while solving the actual task. More recently, OpenAI has halted the release of its GPT-6.1 Astra model8, which appears to be owing to concerns about deceptive behaviour.Recent security incidents with frontier LLMs call for more safety testing but also for a focus on preserving monitorability before further increasing reasoning abilities. While CoT reasoning gives the impression of interpretability, more research is required to understand how LLMs generate reasoning text and how, or whether, it can be used for safety monitoring.
